title: A primary structural binder at global cement scale without process carbon dioxide

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a general-purpose structural binder made from abundant raw materials, at the production volume and regional price of ordinary Portland cement, without releasing carbon dioxide through carbonate decomposition. The binder is the reactive ingredient that binds aggregate into concrete. Success would therefore require a material suitable for ordinary structural construction, together with a manufacturing process and feedstock supply capable of serving a multi-gigatonne market.

Conceptual synthesis: primary production means making new binder from an independently scalable raw-material supply, rather than relying exclusively on previously manufactured cement paste. The target combines material performance, manufacturing chemistry, resource abundance and commodity economics. Eliminating carbonate-decomposition emissions defines the central capability; avoiding fossil-fuel heat is an additional condition in the proposed demonstration. Neither condition alone establishes zero emissions across the complete life cycle or net removal of atmospheric carbon dioxide.

significance.text: Cement manufacture is a major industrial carbon source serving an exceptionally large construction market. Robbie M. Andrew’s dataset description dated 7 October 2025 reports approximately 1.5 Gt CO2 of cement process emissions in 2024, plus approximately 0.9 Gt from fossil fuels used to supply production heat. Those fuel emissions are stated in the description but excluded from the dataset itself. Niu and coauthors’ May 2025 paper describes cement production as contributing up to 8% of anthropogenic CO2 emissions, citing earlier literature, and gives an approximate production-emissions split of 60% from carbonate calcination and 40% from fossil energy. These are dated estimates with different accounting scopes, rather than interchangeable measures of a single total.

If the proposed binder matched Portland cement in structural usefulness, price and available volume, it could enable avoidance of carbonate-decomposition emissions wherever it displaced conventional cement. Meeting the additional condition of fossil-free production heat would address the other major production source. The direct consequence would be a substantially lower-emission binder supply for buildings, bridges, dams and pavements. Technical availability would enable these reductions; realizing them across the industry would require actual deployment and displacement of conventional production.

The scale and price conditions are central to the impact. A useful binder limited to scarce fly ash, blast-furnace slag or other industrial by-products could reduce emissions in particular markets without supplying the global replacement envisaged here. Dunant and coauthors emphasize that Portland cement benefits from raw materials composed of very abundant crustal elements, making comparable cost and volume difficult replacement targets. A new chemistry would also need credible durability and acceptance for structural use before its availability translated into widespread construction.

Conditional implication: a process with no carbonate-decomposition emissions would not automatically produce carbon-negative concrete. Net-negative performance would additionally require atmospheric CO2 uptake exceeding all remaining life-cycle emissions, with credible accounting for the uptake and its persistence. Natural carbonation demonstrates that cementitious materials can absorb CO2, but its existence does not establish that a proposed binder would achieve net removal. Nor would low production emissions alone establish decades of field durability, code acceptance or lower costs for completed structures.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target is an integrated capability: producing a broadly usable structural binder from abundant feedstocks at Portland cement scale and price while avoiding carbonate-decomposition emissions. In their paper published on 22 May 2024, Dunant and coauthors assessed alternative cement chemistries as unable to match that scale and identified an insufficient natural supply of uncarbonated calcium for the required quantities. This documents their assessment at that date. The supplied evidence does not establish whether the combined capability remained unmet on 1 November 2026.

The chemical and resource barriers are connected. Conventional carbonate feedstocks supply calcium while releasing CO2 when decomposed. Avoiding that release requires a different feedstock or reaction pathway, or another means of managing the carbon; changing the equipment or energy source alone does not demonstrate its elimination. Meanwhile, abundant constituent elements do not by themselves establish an economically recoverable feedstock. The route must supply reactive binder ingredients at the required purity, consistency, energy demand and cost. Recovering already-decarbonated cement paste can bypass part of the original chemical burden, but creates a dependence on the availability and recovery of existing material.

Engineering synthesis: the remaining integration challenge includes reliable raw-material preparation, controlled binder production, useful setting and strength development, and durability across the intended structural exposures. These functions must remain economical when feedstock composition varies and output rises to sustained commodity production. Low-cost, low-emission electricity or heat must be available at the required scale, and additives and upstream processing must be included in the emissions assessment. A promising reaction or specimen is therefore only one part of the proposed capability.

current_state.text: Limestone–calcined-clay cement illustrates a substantial reduction in clinker use while retaining Portland clinker. The supplied research attributes to Scrivener and coauthors’ December 2018 LC3 paper clinker contents around 50% with similar mechanical properties. That standalone source was not captured for the supplied review, so the quantitative performance statement remains an attributed research report here. Independently, the retained May 2024 Dunant paper describes these blends as requiring Portland clinker for activation and identifies difficulty in exceeding approximately 50% substitution. This supports clinker reduction, without establishing elimination of calcination emissions or equivalence across every durability requirement.

The supplied research reports laboratory electrochemical decarbonation in Ellis and coauthors’ PNAS study, first published on 16 September 2019 and appearing in the 9 June 2020 issue. It describes prototype electrolyzers producing calcium hydroxide that could react with silica to form alite, an important Portland-clinker mineral. It also describes a concentrated CO2 stream and a subsequent high-temperature clinkering requirement. No saved text of this paper was available to the supplied review, so those experimental details and process requirements could not be independently checked there. The reported advance remains relevant, but it does not establish a commercial primary-binder process with no CO2 release; the disposition of the separated gas and the energy requirements would need to be demonstrated.

Dunant and coauthors’ May 2024 paper experimentally demonstrates reclinkering hydrated or recovered cement paste over molten steel. The reported trials used induction furnaces, clean steel, different crucibles and varying oxidizing conditions. The resulting slag could meet existing Portland-clinker specifications and could be blended with calcined clay and limestone. These results support a recycling route compatible with steelmaking chemistry; they do not establish sustained commercial electric-arc-furnace production or a new primary binder supply.

The electric-recycling route’s zero-emission case depends on already-decarbonated paste and emissions-free electricity. The paper states that recovered cement paste was not commercially available at scale at the time. Co-production with steel recycling would depend on electric-arc-furnace capacity and paste recovery, but scrap-steel throughput is not an absolute limit on every proposed configuration: the authors also propose dedicated cement production in an electric arc furnace retaining a small pool of molten steel. That dedicated configuration is a proposed operating option, while the dependence on recovered paste remains.

Natural carbonation provides a substantial but delayed partial offset to cement emissions. Niu and coauthors’ paper, published on 27 May 2025, estimates global uptake at approximately 0.84 Gt CO2 in 2023, compared with approximately 1.58 Gt of cement process emissions that year, before adding fuel emissions. Much of the uptake occurs in years after the cement is produced. The paper’s conclusion gives 0.83 Gt rather than 0.84 Gt, a small internal discrepancy that supports retaining an approximate figure. These modeled global estimates do not show cancellation of annual process-plus-fuel emissions or establish net-negative performance for a particular new binder.

The evidence establishes dated component advances and emissions estimates, with limits on completeness and currency. Andrew’s October 2025 figures are supported by the supplied dataset landing-page description; the underlying data files were not supplied, and the page flags a newer version. The supplied record contains no freshness search establishing the complete technology landscape as of 1 November 2026. Consequently, it supports neither a claim that the combined innovation has been achieved nor a definitive claim that no subsequent development has achieved it.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration framework: a primary production route should make a binder that passes a recognized general-use cement specification or an explicitly defined equivalent suite covering the intended strength and durability requirements. ASTM C1157 is a candidate specification, but its provisions and applicability must be checked against the standard itself because its text was not supplied. Qualification should make the intended applications, exposure conditions and use restrictions explicit. Passing a finite suite would establish demonstrated breadth within those boundaries, rather than literal suitability for every structural use.
completion_criteria.label: Binder meets general-use specifications within declared application limits

completion_criteria.text: Proposed production and economic demonstration: at least one plant should sustain output on the order of 1 million tonnes per year while producing consistent, specification-conforming material. This is a proposed commercial-scale milestone, not an established threshold or proof of global scalability. The selling price should fall within the relevant regional Portland-cement price band without a permanent operating subsidy, with the assumptions behind the comparison disclosed. A documented feedstock, energy and replication assessment should support expansion toward a multi-gigatonne market without dependence on scarce industrial by-products.
completion_criteria.label: Million-tonne annual production matches regional Portland-cement prices with scalable feedstocks

completion_criteria.text: Proposed emissions demonstration: an independent inventory should cover feedstock preparation, additives and binder manufacture, showing no carbonate-decomposition process emissions and no fossil-fuel heat emissions within that boundary. Electricity-related emissions should be reported separately, alongside other residual upstream emissions. If a route separates a CO2 stream, its eventual disposition and any releases must be included; separation alone would not demonstrate avoidance of emissions. Net atmospheric drawdown would require a further demonstration and is outside the central completion claim.
completion_criteria.label: Independent inventory demonstrates zero carbonate-decomposition and fossil-fuel heat emissions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical validation: independent laboratories should reproduce material-performance results using disclosed methods and representative production batches. Repeated operation with realistic feedstock variability should establish stable output and emissions performance. Field placements and longer-term monitoring should test relevant exposure conditions, with accelerated durability tests treated as supporting evidence rather than automatic proof of decades of service. Code acceptance and application-specific approval remain separate adoption requirements. Together, these demonstrations would establish the capability within declared material, plant and environmental boundaries.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication and field monitoring validate stable production performance

related_concepts.text: Conceptual comparison with the supplied roster: CIV-03, in-place conversion of ordinary ground into a specified engineering solid, overlaps in mineral binding and control of engineering properties. Its defining challenge is transforming ground where it lies, whereas CIV-01 concerns primary manufacture and supply of a structural binder. CIV-07, load-bearing engineered living materials, could overlap if biological processes produced or organized the binder, but living-material function is an additional capability that CIV-01 does not require.

Conceptual comparison: CIV-04, repeated recovery of structural load capacity after cracking, concerns restoring mechanical function after damage. CIV-05, tensile-ductile mineral structures that replace reinforced concrete at ordinary cost, concerns tensile behavior and structural substitution. CIV-11, default-cost reinforcement with carbon-steel behavior and no corrosion in ordinary exposures, concerns the reinforcing material. A low-emission binder could potentially be combined with any of these, but it would not by itself demonstrate healing, tensile ductility or corrosion-free reinforcement.

Conceptual comparison: CIV-02, mechanics-based prediction of earthquake liquefaction and its ground consequences, concerns predictive understanding of soil response. CIV-09, immediate building occupancy after the design earthquake at life-safety cost, concerns whole-building performance and economics. CIV-12, fail-safe adaptive primary structural response at ordinary-building cost, concerns structural adaptation and reliability. CIV-01 could supply construction material for such systems, but its production chemistry does not establish their predictive or structural capabilities.

Conceptual comparison: CIV-06, underground routes and spaces at surface-infrastructure cost, addresses construction-system economics; CIV-08, large-reservoir storage that passes sediment without giving up carryover water, addresses hydraulic and sediment-management performance. Both could use structural concrete, but a new binder would address only one material input. CIV-10, structural concrete that stores building-relevant energy, shares the concrete platform while adding an energy-storage function that does not follow from low-emission binder production.

Conceptual synthesis: the historical description of carbon-negative binding chemistry from abundant waste streams overlaps with CIV-01 but cannot be established as exactly equivalent from the supplied material. It adds a net atmospheric-removal requirement and specifies waste-stream feedstocks, whereas CIV-01 permits an independently scalable primary raw-material supply. Clinker dilution and recovered-paste recycling are also relevant neighboring approaches: they respectively reduce clinker demand and reuse previously manufactured binder. Their contributions can complement primary production without demonstrating the same capability.

change_log.change: Preserved CIV-01 and its title while explaining the binder, primary-production requirement and combined performance, cost and scale target.
change_log.reason: The innovation is an integrated industrial capability; a limitation in one supporting assertion does not invalidate its identity.

change_log.change: Dated Dunant and coauthors’ scale assessment to May 2024 and retained uncertainty about the technology landscape on 1 November 2026.
change_log.reason: A dated assessment and an empty freshness-search record cannot establish continued absence of the capability.

change_log.change: Separated process-emissions avoidance, fossil-free heat, life-cycle emissions and net atmospheric removal, and made industry-wide reductions conditional on deployment.
change_log.reason: These are distinct accounting and adoption claims; technical availability alone would not eliminate the sector’s emissions.

change_log.change: Retained the 2024 emissions figures while identifying their landing-page basis, the exclusion of fuel emissions from the dataset files and the notice of a newer version.
change_log.reason: The description supports the attributed estimates, but the supplied evidence does not include the underlying data files or newer release.

change_log.change: Preserved the reported LC3 and electrochemical details with explicit source-access limitations.
change_log.reason: Neither standalone source was captured for the supplied review. Their reported findings should remain qualified rather than be discarded or presented as independently checked.

change_log.change: Specified induction-furnace experiments for electric paste reclinkering and distinguished them from proposed electric-arc-furnace operation.
change_log.reason: The demonstrated experimental configuration does not establish sustained commercial EAF production.

change_log.change: Replaced an absolute scrap-steel throughput constraint with a conditional co-production constraint and included the proposed dedicated-furnace option.
change_log.reason: Dunant and coauthors propose cement-only operation over retained molten steel, although recovered-paste supply remains necessary.

change_log.change: Described carbonation uptake as a modeled estimate, retained approximately 0.84 Gt for 2023, noted the 0.83 Gt conclusion figure and compared uptake with 1.58 Gt of process emissions.
change_log.reason: This preserves the useful quantitative context without concealing the internal discrepancy or implying cancellation of process-plus-fuel emissions.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed completion framework to cover sustained output, inventory boundaries, independent reproducibility, feedstock variability and field validation.
change_log.reason: A single plant, specimen or specification result would not establish global replication or unrestricted structural suitability.

change_log.change: Treated ASTM C1157 as a candidate requiring verification and retained the million-tonne and price milestones as proposals.
change_log.reason: The standard itself was not supplied, and the selected milestones are not established authoritative thresholds.

change_log.change: Replaced asserted historical equivalence with qualified overlap and explained distinctions from all other supplied roster entries.
change_log.reason: The historical description lacks enough context to establish identity, while the roster concepts address separate capabilities.

unresolved_issues: Whether any development after the dated supplied sources achieved the combined performance, primary-feedstock, price, volume and emissions capability remains unresolved; no freshness search was supplied.

The standalone LC3 source was not captured. Its reported approximately 50% clinker content with similar mechanical properties remains an attributed finding; the retained Dunant paper independently supports clinker retention.
The electrochemical paper was not captured. Its reported prototype results, gas handling and subsequent clinkering requirements remain unverified within the supplied review.
Andrew’s underlying dataset files and the newer version flagged by its landing page were not supplied, so neither a fresh numerical audit nor an update to the October 2025 estimates is possible here.

Niu and coauthors give approximately 0.84 Gt of 2023 carbonation uptake in the abstract and main results and 0.83 Gt in the conclusion. The discrepancy remains unresolved; inconsistent subdivisions have not been used.
ASTM C1157’s applicability to a future binder requires examination of the standard. The proposed production, economic and testing milestones would also need route-specific operational definitions.
The supplied material does not establish exact equivalence between CIV-01 and the historical carbon-negative waste-stream concept. Their relationship is retained as overlap.

No specific candidate primary process is established here as satisfying the proposed criteria; its feedstock economics, energy requirements, durability, replication limits and residual life-cycle emissions would require demonstration.
